title: Gradient descent

sections.title: 6.7 Is it working? The learning curve

html:
Purpose. Gradient descent is the general way to minimize a cost. It trains linear regression, logistic regression and the largest neural networks. If you understand it, you understand how almost every model in this book learns.

Key ideas

  • Start with any w and b, then repeatedly take a small step downhill on the cost.
  • The step direction comes from the derivative (the slope). The step size is set by the learning rate alpha.
  • Update all parameters at the same time.
  • Alpha too small is slow. Alpha too large overshoots and can make the cost grow.
  • The learning curve (cost against iterations) tells you whether training works.

6.1 The idea

Imagine you are walking down a dark valley with a torch that lights only your feet. You cannot see the bottom, but you can feel which way the ground slopes. So you take a small step in the steepest downhill direction, feel the slope again, and repeat. Ng's picture is a hilly golf course: stand on a hill, turn all the way round, take a baby step in the steepest downhill direction, repeat. You end up at the bottom of a valley.

6.2 The update rule

w:=w−α∂J(w,b)∂wb:=b−α∂J(w,b)∂bw := w - \alpha \frac{\partial J(w,b)}{\partial w} \qquad b := b - \alpha \frac{\partial J(w,b)}{\partial b}
  • The sign := means "assign", as in code. It is not a claim that both sides are equal.
  • alpha is the learning rate, a small positive number such as 0.01. It sets the size of each step.
  • The derivative is the slope of the cost in that direction. If the slope is positive (uphill to the right), subtracting it moves w to the left. If the slope is negative, w moves right. Either way you move towards the bottom.
  • Update w and b simultaneously: compute both new values from the old ones first, then assign them. Updating w first and then using the new w to compute b's step is a subtle bug.

When you reach the minimum the slope is 0, so the update changes nothing: the algorithm has converged. Even with a fixed alpha, the steps shrink on their own near the bottom because the slope shrinks.

6.3 The derivatives for linear regression

Calculus gives (Ng, video 19):

∂J∂w=1m∑i=1m(fw,b(x(i))−y(i))x(i)∂J∂b=1m∑i=1m(fw,b(x(i))−y(i))\frac{\partial J}{\partial w} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( f_{w,b}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right) x^{(i)} \qquad \frac{\partial J}{\partial b} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left( f_{w,b}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right)

In words: the step for b is the average error. The step for w is the average of the error times the input, so examples with large inputs have more say about w. The 2 from differentiating the square cancels the 1/2 in the cost.

6.4 A worked example, by hand

Take the three points (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), start at w = 0, b = 0, and use alpha = 0.1.

  • Predictions: 0, 0, 0. Errors f - y: -1, -2, -3. The cost is 2.333.
  • dJ/dw = (1/3) x (-1 x 1 + -2 x 2 + -3 x 3) = -14/3 = -4.667. dJ/db = (1/3) x (-1 - 2 - 3) = -2.
  • New w = 0 - 0.1 x (-4.667) = 0.467. New b = 0 - 0.1 x (-2) = 0.2.
  • The new cost is 0.470, down from 2.333.

Repeating gives, after steps 2, 3, 4, 5: w = 0.676, 0.770, 0.813, 0.833 and costs 0.101, 0.027, 0.012, 0.009. After 2,000 steps it reaches w = 1.0 and b = 0.0. The cost falls fastest at the start, when the slope is steepest, and then crawls.

6.5 Code from scratch

Same fifty points as in Chapter 4:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 50)
y = 3 * x + 2 + rng.normal(0, 1, 50)

def gradient_descent(x, y, alpha, steps):
    w, b = 0.0, 0.0
    history = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        err = w * x + b - y                  # prediction minus target, for every example
        dw = (err * x).mean()                # both derivatives use the OLD w and b
        db = err.mean()
        w, b = w - alpha * dw, b - alpha * db   # simultaneous update
        history.append((err ** 2).mean() / 2)   # cost before this step
    return w, b, history

w, b, history = gradient_descent(x, y, alpha=0.05, steps=500)
print(round(w, 3), round(b, 3))   # 3.053 1.753  (the formula gave 3.052 1.757)

Gradient descent lands within 0.004 of the exact answer from the formula.

6.6 Choosing the learning rate

On this data, after 500 steps:

Alpha Result What it means
0.001 w = 3.220, b = 0.613 Still moving: too small, too slow
0.01 w = 3.112, b = 1.350 Closer, still not there
0.05 w = 3.053, b = 1.753 Converged
0.1 w grows without bound Too large: each step overshoots further than the last

If the learning rate is too large, a step jumps over the bottom and lands higher on the other side, then jumps back even further. The cost grows on every step. If it is too small, training is correct but you may wait forever.

6.7 Is it working? The learning curve

Plot the cost J after every iteration (not against w or b). This is the learning curve (Ng, video 27).

  • If gradient descent works, J goes down on every single iteration.
  • If J ever goes up, alpha is too large, or there is a bug. A classic bug is writing w + alpha x slope instead of minus.
  • When the curve flattens, training has converged. The number of iterations needed can be 30 for one problem and 100,000 for another, so you cannot know in advance.
  • An automatic test: stop when J falls by less than a tiny epsilon (such as 0.001) in one iteration. Ng finds it hard to choose epsilon, so he prefers to look at the graph.
  • Debugging tip: set alpha to a very small number. J must then fall on every iteration. If it does not, the code has a bug. A tiny alpha is for debugging, not for real training.
  • Choosing alpha: try values about three times apart: 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1. Run a few iterations of each, plot the curves, and pick the largest value that still falls steadily, or one slightly smaller.

6.8 Batch, stochastic and mini-batch

Beyond the videos. The version above uses all m examples for every step. That is batch gradient descent (Ng, video 20). For millions of examples it is slow, so practitioners compute the slope on a random small group of examples per step: stochastic gradient descent uses one example, mini-batch uses a few (often 32 to 256). Steps become noisier, but far cheaper, and the model still converges. Neural networks are almost always trained with mini-batches and an improved version of gradient descent called Adam, which adapts the step size for each parameter.

Loan example. Training the monthly-cost model from a table of offers is exactly this loop: predict, measure the gap to the real monthly cost, compute the two slopes, nudge w and b, repeat until the learning curve is flat.

Common mistakes

  • Updating w and b one after the other instead of simultaneously.
  • Choosing alpha by a single guess and never plotting the learning curve.
  • Plus instead of minus in the update.
  • Running gradient descent on unscaled features and wondering why it is slow (Chapter 8).

Check yourself

  • A slope is positive. In which direction does w move, and why?
  • You see the cost going up and down on successive iterations. Name two possible causes.
  • Why does gradient descent slow down near the minimum even if alpha does not change?
  • Do one step by hand for the points (1, 2), (2, 4) from w = 0, b = 0 with alpha = 0.1. What are w and b afterwards?
Show answers

(1) w moves left, to smaller values, because w := w - alpha x slope and the slope is positive. (2) Alpha is too large (overshooting), or a bug such as a sign error. (3) The slope shrinks as you approach the bottom, so each step is smaller. (4) Errors are -2 and -4; dw = (1/2)(-2 x 1 + -4 x 2) = -5, db = (1/2)(-2 - 4) = -3; so w = 0.5 and b = 0.3.
